Algal_Leaf_Spot.description: Algal Leaf Spot is caused by a parasitic green alga called Cephaleuros virescens. It appears as circular to irregular orange-red or rusty-brown spots on the upper surface of leaves. The disease is common in humid tropical and subtropical regions and primarily affects the leaves and sometimes stems of jackfruit trees.
symptoms: Circular or irregular orange-red to rusty-brown spots on upper leaf surface
Velvety or powdery appearance on the spot surface due to algal growth
Spots range from 2mm to 2cm in diameter
Yellowing of leaf tissue around the spots
Premature leaf drop in severe infections
Reduced photosynthesis leading to poor fruit quality
causes: Parasitic green alga Cephaleuros virescens
High humidity and waterlogged conditions
Poor air circulation within the canopy
Weakened trees due to nutritional deficiency
Rainy seasons with prolonged wet periods
Algal_Leaf_Spot.severity: Moderate — Can cause significant defoliation if untreated
treatment: Spray copper-based fungicides (Copper Oxychloride 50% WP at 3g/L water)
Apply Bordeaux mixture (1%) every 15 days during wet season
Remove and destroy severely infected leaves
Spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5g/L water as an alternative
Repeat spraying after rainfall
prevention: Prune trees regularly to improve air circulation
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip irrigation instead
Apply balanced fertilizers especially potassium to strengthen plant immunity
Remove fallen infected leaves from the ground
Maintain proper spacing between trees
Apply preventive copper sprays at the start of rainy season

Black_Spot.description: Black Spot in Jackfruit is a fungal disease that causes dark black or brown necrotic lesions on leaves, stems, and fruits. It is particularly damaging during post-harvest and can spread rapidly under humid conditions. The disease significantly reduces marketable fruit quality and can cause premature fruit drop.
symptoms: Small black or dark brown circular spots on leaves
Spots enlarge and may merge to form large necrotic areas
Water-soaked lesions in early stages
Dark sunken lesions on fruits causing post-harvest losses
Premature defoliation in severe cases
Pink spore masses visible on spots under humid conditions
causes: Fungal pathogens Colletotrichum gloeosporioides or Phomopsis sp.
High humidity (above 80%) and warm temperatures (25-30°C)
Wounds on plant surface from insects or pruning
Poor sanitation and infected plant debris
Infected planting material
Black_Spot.severity: High — Can cause complete crop loss if untreated
treatment: Apply Carbendazim 50% WP at 1g/L water every 10-14 days
Spray Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP at 1.5g/L water
Use Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 2g/L water as broad-spectrum fungicide
Remove and burn all infected plant parts immediately
Post-harvest treatment with hot water (52°C for 5 minutes) for fruits
prevention: Use disease-free certified planting material
Avoid creating wounds during pruning — sterilize tools
Maintain good drainage around tree base
Apply preventive fungicide sprays before monsoon season
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves and fruits
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Black_Spot.recovery_chance: Moderate — Early detection critical. Above 60% infection, recovery unlikely

Cutting_Weevil.description: The Mango Cutting Weevil is an insect pest where adult weevils cut young shoots and tender leaves. The female weevil cuts a young shoot partially, rolls the leaf into a cigar-shaped tube, lays eggs inside, and the cut shoot falls to the ground. This causes significant loss of young shoots especially during the flushing season.
symptoms: Young shoots cut partially and hanging or fallen on ground
Leaves rolled into cigar-shaped tubes (egg-laying sites)
Wilting and drying of cut shoots
Tiny puncture marks on young tender leaves
Presence of adult weevils (3-4mm, black with white markings) on shoots
Severe dieback of young growth during flushing season
causes: Adult weevil Deporaus marginatus
Peak activity during new flush/shoot emergence
Warm humid conditions favor weevil population
Dense canopy providing shelter for pests
Nearby infested trees spreading the pest
Cutting_Weevil.severity: High during flush season — Can destroy entire new growth
treatment: Spray Chlorpyriphos 20% EC at 2mL/L water when new flush appears
Apply Imidacloprid 17.8% SL at 0.5mL/L water as systemic insecticide
Use Quinalphos 25% EC at 2mL/L water
Collect and destroy fallen cut shoots daily to break pest cycle
Apply Neem-based insecticide (Azadirachtin 0.03%) at 5mL/L water as organic option
prevention: Monitor trees regularly during flushing season
Collect and destroy rolled leaf tubes containing eggs
Apply preventive insecticide spray before new flush emergence
Remove weeds and alternate hosts near mango trees
Encourage natural predators by avoiding broad-spectrum pesticides
Prune dense canopy to reduce shelter for weevils
Cutting_Weevil.recovery_chance: High if treated promptly — New flush will emerge after treatment
Cutting_Weevil.source: Pakistan Agriculture Research Council, CABI Plantwise

Gall_Midge.description: Mango Gall Midge is a serious insect pest caused by tiny flies whose larvae create galls (abnormal growths) on mango leaves, petioles, and sometimes flowers and young fruits. The larvae feed inside the plant tissue causing distortion and gall formation. Heavy infestation can severely reduce tree vigor and fruit production.
symptoms: Small green to brown galls (swellings) on leaf surface
Leaf curling and distortion
Galls on petioles causing leaf drop
Abnormal swellings on young stems
Galls on flower stalks reducing fruit set
Yellowing of infested leaves
causes: Gall midge fly Erosomyia mangiferae
Larvae feeding inside plant tissue
Peak infestation during new flush and flowering
High humidity and moderate temperatures (20-28°C)
Dense planting allowing pest spread
Gall_Midge.severity: High — Can cause 30-70% reduction in yield
treatment: Spray Dimethoate 30% EC at 2mL/L water during new flush
Apply Phosphamidon 40% SL at 1.5mL/L water
Use Systemic insecticide Thiamethoxam 25% WG at 0.3g/L water
Remove and destroy galled plant parts
Soil application of Chlorpyriphos 20% EC (10mL/tree) to kill pupating larvae
prevention: Regular monitoring during flushing and flowering
Prune and destroy infested shoots immediately
Rake and remove soil around tree base to expose pupae
Apply preventive spray 2 weeks before expected flush
Maintain tree health through proper fertilization
Inter-crop with plants that harbor natural enemies
Gall_Midge.recovery_chance: Moderate — Multiple treatments needed. Above 60% galling, season is lost
Gall_Midge.source: CABI Plantwise, FAO Mango Production Guidelines

Die_Back.description: Die Back is one of the most serious fungal diseases of mango. The fungus invades through wounds and causes progressive death of shoots and branches from the tip backward. It can spread to major branches and the trunk, eventually killing the entire tree. The disease is particularly severe in stressed trees.
symptoms: Drying and dying of shoot tips progressing downward
Dark brown to black discoloration under bark of infected shoots
Leaves turn brown and remain attached to dead shoots
Gum exudation from infected branches
Dark streaks in wood when branch is cut
Entire branch death in advanced stages
Cankers on main stem in severe cases
causes: Fungus Lasiodiplodia theobromae entering through wounds
Pruning wounds left untreated
Sunburn damage on branches
Drought stress weakening tree immunity
Insect damage creating entry points
Die_Back.severity: Very High — Can kill entire tree if untreated. Recovery impossible above 60% infection
treatment: Prune infected shoots 15-20cm below visible infection
Paint all pruning wounds immediately with Bordeaux paste or Copper Oxychloride
Spray Carbendazim 50% WP at 1g/L water on pruned areas
Apply Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP at 1.5g/L water
Trunk injection with Tridemorph in severe cases
Remove severely infected trees to prevent spread
prevention: Always paint pruning wounds with fungicide paste immediately
Avoid creating unnecessary wounds on trees
Maintain adequate irrigation — drought stress increases susceptibility
Apply balanced fertilizer especially potassium and phosphorus
Remove and burn dead wood immediately
Sterilize pruning tools between trees with 70% alcohol
Die_Back.recovery_chance: Low to None above 60% infection — Early detection is critical
Die_Back.source: Pakistan Agriculture Research Council, CABI Die Back Management

Sooty_Mould.description: Sooty Mould is a fungal disease that grows on the honeydew secreted by sucking insects like mealybugs, scale insects, and aphids. The black sooty coating covers leaf surfaces, blocking sunlight and reducing photosynthesis. It is a secondary disease — controlling the honeydew-producing insects is the primary solution.
symptoms: Black sooty coating on upper surface of leaves
Coating can be wiped off with fingers (unlike other diseases)
Reduced leaf shine and dark appearance of entire canopy
Presence of sucking insects (mealybugs, scales, aphids) on undersides of leaves
Stunted growth due to reduced photosynthesis
Black coating on young fruits reducing market value
causes: Fungus growing on honeydew from sucking pests
Mealybugs (Drosicha mangiferae) — primary culprit in Pakistan
Scale insects and aphids also produce honeydew
High humidity favoring fungal growth
Dense canopy reducing air movement
Sooty_Mould.severity: Moderate — Mainly reduces yield quality and photosynthesis
treatment: First: Control sucking insects with Imidacloprid 17.8% SL at 0.5mL/L water
Apply Dimethoate 30% EC at 2mL/L water for mealybug control
Wash leaves with water to physically remove sooty mould
Spray starch solution (2%) to strip mould coating
Apply Copper Oxychloride 50% WP at 3g/L water after pest control
Use sticky bands on tree trunks to prevent ant-mealybug mutualism
prevention: Control sucking insect populations before honeydew production
Apply sticky bands on tree trunks to block ants carrying mealybugs
Prune to improve air circulation
Encourage natural predators (ladybirds, lacewings)
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which attracts sucking pests
Regular monitoring for sucking insects especially before mango season
Sooty_Mould.recovery_chance: High — Once insects are controlled, new leaves will be clean
Sooty_Mould.source: CABI Plantwise, Pakistan Mango Research Institute

Powdery_Mildew.description: Powdery Mildew is one of the most destructive diseases of mango, particularly affecting the flowering and fruiting stages. The fungus produces white powdery growth on flowers, young fruits, and leaves. It is most devastating during the flowering season and can cause complete crop failure if not managed.
symptoms: White powdery coating on flowers, young leaves, and fruits
Infected flowers turn brown and drop prematurely
Young fruits develop white coating and drop
Distortion of affected plant parts
Severe flower and fruit drop leading to crop loss
Leaves show white patches that later turn brown
causes: Fungus Oidium mangiferae
Cool nights and warm days (15-20°C nights, 25-30°C days)
High relative humidity without rain (unlike other fungal diseases)
Dense canopy with poor air movement
Peak infection during flowering season (January-March in Pakistan)
Powdery_Mildew.severity: Very High — Can cause 80-100% crop loss during severe outbreaks
treatment: Spray Sulphur 80% WP at 3g/L water — most effective and economical
Apply Hexaconazole 5% SC at 2mL/L water
Use Myclobutanil 10% WP at 1g/L water for severe infections
Spray Tebuconazole 25.9% EC at 1mL/L water
Start treatment at first sign of powdery coating
Repeat every 10-15 days during flowering
prevention: Apply preventive sulphur spray before flowering begins
Prune trees to improve air circulation
Apply first spray when panicles (flower clusters) are just emerging
Avoid late evening irrigation during flowering
Monitor weather forecasts — spray before predicted cool humid nights
Remove and destroy infected plant parts
Powdery_Mildew.recovery_chance: High if treated at early stage. During peak flowering, immediate action essential
Powdery_Mildew.source: Pakistan Agriculture Research Council, CABI Mango Disease Management

Bacterial_Leaf_Spot.description: Bacterial Leaf Spot of Pumpkin is caused by Xanthomonas bacteria and is one of the most common and damaging diseases of cucurbits including pumpkin, squash, and cucumber. The bacteria enter through stomata and wounds, causing water-soaked lesions that turn yellow-brown and eventually die.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves, initially appearing greasy
Spots turn yellow then brown with angular shape (limited by leaf veins)
Yellow halo surrounding brown lesions
Lesions may tear giving leaves a ragged appearance
Spots on fruits appear dark and water-soaked
Fruit rotting in severe infections
causes: Bacteria Xanthomonas campestris pv. cucurbitae
Spread through water splash, rain, and contaminated tools
High humidity and warm temperatures (24-30°C)
Wounds from insects or mechanical damage
Infected seeds spreading to new plants
Bacterial_Leaf_Spot.severity: High — Rapidly spreads under wet conditions. Major yield loss possible
treatment: Spray Copper Hydroxide 77% WP at 2.5g/L water every 7-10 days
Apply Copper Oxychloride 50% WP at 3g/L water
Use Streptomycin Sulphate 90% SP at 0.5g/L water (antibiotic)
Combine copper + streptomycin for better control
Remove and destroy severely infected leaves
Avoid working in field when plants are wet
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or treat seeds with hot water (50°C, 25 min)
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip irrigation
Maintain 2-3 year crop rotation with non-cucurbit crops
Remove crop debris after harvest
Sterilize tools between plants
Avoid working in wet fields to prevent spread
Bacterial_Leaf_Spot.recovery_chance: Moderate — Control possible if caught early. Poor prognosis above 60% infection
Bacterial_Leaf_Spot.source: FAO Cucurbit Disease Management, CABI Plantwise

Downy_Mildew.description: Downy Mildew is one of the most economically important diseases of cucurbits worldwide. It is caused by a water mold and spreads rapidly under cool, wet conditions. The disease can devastate entire pumpkin crops within days under favorable conditions. It is distinct from Powdery Mildew — it appears on undersides of leaves.
symptoms: Yellow angular spots on upper leaf surface (limited by veins)
Purple-grey to brown downy growth on underside of leaves
Rapid leaf yellowing and browning
Leaves wilt and die rapidly
Disease spreads very fast in the field
Defoliation leaving fruits unprotected from sunburn
causes: Water mold Pseudoperonospora cubensis
Cool temperatures (15-20°C) with high humidity
Free moisture on leaves for at least 6 hours
Spores spread by wind over long distances
Overhead irrigation wetting leaves
Downy_Mildew.severity: Very High — Can destroy entire crop within 1-2 weeks under favorable conditions
treatment: Spray Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP at 2.5g/L water — most effective
Apply Dimethomorph 50% WP at 1.5g/L water
Use Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP at 2.5g/L water
Spray Fosetyl-Al 80% WP at 2.5g/L water as systemic treatment
Alternate between different fungicide groups to prevent resistance
Apply every 5-7 days during outbreak
prevention: Use resistant pumpkin varieties where available
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip irrigation
Improve air circulation by proper plant spacing
Apply preventive fungicide sprays before disease appears during cool wet weather
Monitor weather — spray before predicted rainy cool periods
Remove infected plant debris from field
Downy_Mildew.recovery_chance: Low above 50% infection — Speed of response is critical
Downy_Mildew.source: FAO Cucurbit Disease Guidelines, CABI Downy Mildew Management

Mosaic_Disease.scientific_name: Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W) / Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV)
Mosaic_Disease.description: Mosaic Disease in pumpkin is caused by viral pathogens transmitted by aphids. The virus causes characteristic mosaic (mixed light and dark green) patterns on leaves, leaf distortion, and stunted growth. There is NO CURE for viral diseases — infected plants must be removed to prevent spread. Prevention through aphid control is the only management strategy.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern — irregular light and dark green areas on leaves
Leaf curling, puckering, and distortion
Stunted plant growth
Small, misshapen fruits with discoloration
Fruits show yellow-green irregular patches
Reduced fruit set and quality
causes: Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W) or Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV)
Transmitted by aphids (especially Aphis gossypii) in non-persistent manner
Infected plant debris and nearby infected cucurbits
Contaminated tools in some cases
No seed transmission in most strains
Mosaic_Disease.severity: Very High — NO CURE. Infected plants must be removed immediately
treatment: ⚠️ NO CHEMICAL CURE EXISTS FOR VIRAL DISEASES
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent aphid spread
Control aphid vectors with Imidacloprid 17.8% SL at 0.5mL/L water
Apply Mineral oil spray (1%) to reduce aphid landing and virus transmission
Remove all infected crop residue after harvest
Reflective mulches confuse aphids and reduce virus spread
prevention: Control aphid populations before they transmit virus
Use reflective silver mulch to deter aphids
Plant resistant or tolerant varieties where available
Maintain 500m distance from other infected cucurbit crops
Remove weeds that harbor aphids and virus
Early planting to avoid peak aphid season
Monitor regularly and remove infected plants immediately
Mosaic_Disease.recovery_chance: None — Viral disease has no cure. Remove infected plants immediately to save neighbors
Mosaic_Disease.source: FAO Virus Disease Management, CABI Cucurbit Virus Guidelines

Red_Rot.description: Red Rot is one of the most destructive fungal diseases of sugarcane. It reddens internal stalk tissue with white or silvery patches and produces a sour or alcoholic smell. External symptoms appear late, so by the time leaves yellow or the crown shows spindle infection, internal damage is often already severe.
symptoms: Reddening of internal stalk tissue with white/silvery patches when cane is split
Distinct sour or alcoholic smell from infected stalks
Yellowing of leaves in advanced stages
Spindle infection visible at the crown
Drying and death of affected clumps
Reduced cane and sugar yield
causes: Fungus Colletotrichum falcatum
Humid and rainy weather favoring spread
Infected seed cane (setts) used for planting
Waterlogging and poor field drainage
Wounds and stressed plants increasing susceptibility
Red_Rot.severity: Very High — Can wipe out an entire plantation under favorable conditions
treatment: Apply Carbendazim 50% WP at about 1g/L water as a soil drench around affected clumps
Dip cane setts in 1% Bordeaux mixture or fungicide solution before planting
Remove and burn affected clumps immediately — do not compost infected material
Avoid further planting from infected fields
Improve drainage to reduce fungal spread
prevention: Use only healthy, disease-free seed cane (setts)
Plant resistant sugarcane varieties where available
Practice crop rotation and avoid waterlogging
Remove and destroy infected clumps promptly
Avoid taking planting material from fields with red rot history
Maintain field sanitation after harvest
Red_Rot.recovery_chance: Low once infection is established — Early rogueing and clean planting material are critical
Red_Rot.source: Pakistan Agriculture Research Council, CABI Plantwise

Yellow_Disease.description: Yellow Leaf Disease is a viral infection of sugarcane caused by Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus. It starts with intense yellowing of the leaf midrib and can progress to stunted growth, shortened internodes, and a bunchy-top appearance. There is no chemical cure — management is entirely preventive.
symptoms: Intense yellowing of the leaf midrib, often visible on the underside first
Yellowing starting on leaves 3-6 counting down from the top
Yellowing spreading into the leaf blade as disease progresses
Stunted growth with shortened internodes
Bunchy-top appearance in severe cases
Early symptoms easily mistaken for nutrient deficiency or ageing
causes: Sugarcane Yellow Leaf Virus (ScYLV)
Transmission by aphids such as Melanaphis sacchari
Use of infected seed cane
Fields with a history of yellow leaf disease
Uncontrolled aphid populations spreading the virus
Yellow_Disease.severity: High — Can reduce cane yield by up to 50% and sugar/juice yield by 40-50%
treatment: No chemical cure exists for viral infection
Rogue out (remove) severely infected plants to reduce virus reservoir
Control aphid vectors with an appropriate insecticide
Do not take planting material from infected plants or fields
Replace severely affected stools with certified virus-free seed cane
prevention: Use only certified virus-free seed cane (tissue-culture-derived where possible)
Control aphid populations (Melanaphis sacchari), the primary vector
Rogue severely infected plants early
Avoid planting material from fields with yellow leaf disease history
Monitor regularly for midrib yellowing
Maintain good crop hygiene between seasons
Yellow_Disease.recovery_chance: None for infected plants — Prevention and virus-free planting material are the only reliable strategy
Yellow_Disease.source: Pakistan Agriculture Research Council, CABI Plantwise

Healthy.description: The plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease. The plant has not crossed the critical 60% infection threshold. Continue regular monitoring and preventive care to maintain plant health.
symptoms: No disease symptoms visible
Normal green leaf color
No spots, lesions, or abnormal growth
Healthy shoot and leaf development
causes: N/A — Plant is healthy
treatment: No treatment required at this time
prevention: Continue regular monitoring every 7-10 days
Maintain proper irrigation and drainage
Apply balanced fertilizer (NPK) as per crop requirement
Keep field clean of weeds and crop debris
Apply preventive copper spray at start of rainy season
Control insect pests before they cause damage
Healthy.recovery_chance: N/A — Plant is currently healthy. Early monitoring is key to keeping it healthy
